reviewer: Claude Code (AI assistant). Not an independent human review.
method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1789, and of 1788 where they reach the 1789 pages (long-running ones included), every item in 3 or more papers counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page, papers that comparison missed looked for again and read, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for items the families miss, phrase searches on all 742 pages of 1789 in both transcriptions for every admitted item, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, the others chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; in 1789, with four papers, every eligible item is printed by all four and admitted)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: London, 9 April 1789: 'A most outrageous tumult has happened at Barcelona, in Spain, in consequence of the high price of bread'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report among the London news of 9 April 1789 (the New-Hampshire papers introduce it with 'says a late European paper'): 'A most outrageous tumult has happened at Barcelona, in Spain, in consequence of the high price of bread. On the 1st ult. a very numerous mob began to set fire to the town magazines, where the corn is deposited. Having finished here, they burnt two houses belonging to principal corn dealers, besides some others.' The papers give the day as 'the 1st ult.', 'the first of April' and 'the first instant'; the Kentucky Gazette prints a longer text. Counted by its own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1789 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: An Act for establishing an Executive Department, to be denominated the Department of Foreign Affairs, approved 27 July 1789
new_groups.definition: Printings of the act of Congress approved on 27 July 1789, as the papers print it from the laws of the first session ('Congress of the United States. Begun and held at the City of New-York, on Wednesday the Fourth of March, One Thousand Seven Hundred and Eighty-Nine'): 'An ACT for establishing an Executive Department, to be denominated the Department of Foreign Affairs. BE it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That there shall be an executive department, to be denominated the department of foreign affairs, and that there shall be a principal officer therein, to be called the Secretary for the department of foreign affairs ...'. Lists of the session's acts that give only its title, and the Senate's journal naming the bill, are not counted (C-07).

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1789 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json). The same script was run with year 1788 over the 1789 pages (items_from_1788.json). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1789 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (74 texts). For every text at the bar or one paper short of it, the papers the comparison missed were looked for again on their pages (the best page within the text's weeks) and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09); each was read. The acts of Congress were counted act by act, a page counting when it prints the act's enacting words, not only its title. Every admitted item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 742 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. 1789 has four papers, so an item reaches the bar only when all four print it: every eligible item is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks and is admitted, and nothing is chosen. The fourth paper, the New-Hampshire Gazetteer, survives from 18 August, so no item reaches the bar unless it was still being printed after that day.
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1789 has 5 catalogue series, which are 4 papers: the Kentucky Gazette (Lexington) is under two numbers, 'The Kentucke gazette' (sn82014784) to 7 March and 'The Kentucky gazette' (sn82014782) from 14 March (C-04), and 46 of its 47 issues are scanned twice (filed as editions 1 and 2; C-05: each printing is counted once, on the first scan). The New-Hampshire Gazette and General Advertiser (Portsmouth; 51 issues) and the Kentucky Gazette (Saturdays) run all year; the Gazette of the United States (New York, Wednesdays and Saturdays; 73 issues) from 15 April; the New-Hampshire Gazetteer (Exeter, Saturdays; 15 issues) from 18 August. Papers in print in any three weeks: 2 from January to mid-April, 3 to the end of July, and all 4 from the windows that reach 18 August.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The six admitted items are each printed by all four papers, counted by phrase searches of their openings and every hit read; their papers are in the README's table of stories. The items read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.A report inside a longer paragraph: The report from Croatia stands inside a Vienna paragraph of 13 May in three papers, after a report that the Emperor is ill; the Kentucky Gazette prints it alone under the dateline. It is counted by its own opening sentence (as 1782 counted the Charlestown report of Savannah's evacuation inside a longer paragraph): 4 of 4. The report that the Emperor is ill is in 3 of 4. The letter from Ancona is a one-sentence report inside London paragraphs of 10 June (the Gazette of the United States and the Kentucky Gazette) and 15 June (the New-Hampshire papers), counted by its own words.
counted_item_by_item.The acts of Congress: Each act is its own item, counted where its enacting words are printed. Lists of the session's acts, which give only their titles (the Gazette of the United States of 3 October, the New-Hampshire Gazette of 15 October and the Kentucky Gazette of 28 November), and the Senate's journal naming its bills are not counted (C-07). Only the act for the Department of Foreign Affairs is printed by all four papers; five more are printed by three.
counted_item_by_item.The amendments to the Constitution: Three texts, each counted by its own opening: the report of the House's committee of 28 July (2 of 4), the House's seventeen articles of 24 August (2 of 4: the Gazette of the United States and the Kentucky Gazette, 28 November) and the twelve articles both Houses proposed to the states in September, with their preamble (3 of 4: the Gazette of the United States, the New-Hampshire Gazetteer and the New-Hampshire Gazette). The House's debates in committee, which quote the committee's articles one by one, are not counted (C-07).
counted_item_by_item.Second scans: The Kentucky Gazette's second scans (edition 2) hold the same issues and are not counted again (C-05); its issue of 3 January survives only as edition 2.

for_user_decision.The floor of four papers before 18 Augus: As built: before 18 August only three papers survive (from January to mid-April only two), so no item first printed then reaches the bar of 4 unless the New-Hampshire Gazetteer still prints it after that day. The President's speech at his inauguration (30 April) is printed by all three papers that survive for its weeks and is not eligible. Five of the six admitted items were first printed between 25 July and 5 August and reach 4 papers because the Gazetteer reprinted them.
for_user_decision.The amendments to the Constitution: As built: the twelve articles both Houses proposed to the states are in 3 of 4 papers by their own words, below the bar; the Kentucky Gazette prints the House's seventeen articles of 24 August instead (28 November). Counted together, as one proposal in two printed forms (C-02), they would be in 4 of 4 and admitted by the first part.
for_user_decision.A report inside a longer paragraph: As built: the report from Croatia is counted by its own opening sentence and admitted (4 of 4). Counted as part of the Vienna paragraph, which opens with the report that the Emperor is ill, it would be in 3 of 4 (the Kentucky Gazette prints only the second report), below the bar, as 1782 counted extracts without their opening (X-1782-05).
for_user_decision.The proceedings of the House: As built (C-09): the House's proceedings, which the Gazette of the United States reported and the other three papers reprinted in parts, are runs of a day's business; the days of 11 August and 16 September are in all four papers and are not admitted.
